Kenshi is ugly, opaque, confusing, buggy, and unwelcoming. It demands patience and persistence with no immediate rewards. It makes no allowances for the inexperienced, the inept, or the videogame-illiterate. It actively defies you to give up and uninstall within the first 10 minutes of play. It also happens to be a little bit brilliant.

Having vaguely followed Kenshi's development for years, and having bounced hard off the free demo released a few years ago, I finally picked it up on sale, confident that I would probably Steam refund it after my second try. One week later and I've hardly played anything else.  

It's quite likely you're suffering a little cognitive dissonance as your eyes drift from the rather unpromising screenshots and trailers - packed with outdated graphics, an ugly UI, and vague, overambitious-sounding statements - to the Steam reviews, which are currently 87% positive. You may be worried that Kenshi is one of those games that is really enjoyable for hardcore, min-maxing basement dwellers but totally inaccessible to anyone else - and that's a legitimate concern. Kenshi [i]does[/i] ask you to invest time and patience to get the most out of it; I want to convince you that the investment is worthwhile.

As the trailers suggest, you start off as a nobody in a harsh, post-apocalyptic world filled with people (and monsters) that comprehensively outnumber, outgun, and outclass you. And that's it. There's not a main quest that doles out steadily-improving powers and gear, there's not a friendly NPC who gives you some cash and directions to an easy fight with decent loot. You exist in a hostile world that can and will kill you moments after leaving the starter town - it's how you bounce back and start making that world your own that makes Kenshi stand out.

There's a moment of existential dread that sets in when you look out over the scorched wasteland, with nothing more than some rags, a rusty iron stick, and half a day's food in your pack, wondering what the hell to do next and if it's even worth it. [i]Fight through that dread[/i]. That feeling of aimlessness and hopelessness is just mainstream-videogames leaving your system; you get so used to a smooth tutorial and a clear path ahead that all the freedom in front of you is straight-up daunting. What should you do? [i]Just start walking[/i]. 

The world of Kenshi is huge, and contains rather more colour and diversity than the trailers make out. There are roaming bands of marauders, mutants, cannibals and religious zealots, there are fortified cities, hardscrabble farmsteads, and infested ruins, there are foetid swamps, blasted deserts, and weird, fungal valleys just as peculiar and intriguing as anything out of Morrowind. When you start out, this world is going to reject you: there's nothing you can face in a straight fight and nowhere safe to lay down roots. To get anywhere, you'll have to sneak, steal, starve, and - yes - get the shit kicked out of you every now and then. 

Life at the bottom of the food chain is tough, and it can feel like you're not making progress, but in reality everything you do is making you tougher. Getting walloped makes your character hardier, losing fights improves your combat skills, and the scraps you pick from the aftermath of procedural battles between NPCs can provide some much-needed gear. In my first few days, I scrounged up enough money for the materials to put up a small shack. I built it away from civilisation, tucked into the crevices of a mountain by the swamp, hoping maybe to scratch out a living by farming before venturing out and doing some walloping of my own.

Bandits came and beat me up. Raptors ate my first crop, then my second crop - then every harvest after that for a week. Desperate, I wandered deeper into the swamp, looting the remains of swamp bandits who had been eaten by blood spiders (blood spiders?!) as I went. I found a settlement, pawned my paltry pickings, and signed on a couple of outcasts willing to join me for free. Back to the shack we went, where once again the raptors ate our crops and the bandits doled out humiliating beatings. The next time they came back there was a wall, and a big gate. They just knocked down the gate. The time after that, there were crossbows mounted on the walls and a few more drifters on our side.  They got through the gate, but no farther. We do the walloping now.

Kenshi erects some fairly high barriers around itself, and a lot of the best fights and features are locked behind those barriers. This starts out feeling like a problem, but you come to realise that overcoming those barriers make every success, no matter how minor, seem immensely important. The struggle to survive never stops being real, and no threats ever become so trivial that they can be safely dismissed. This means you are invested in your characters and in the world in a way you rarely feel in other games; by the time you get a handle on things, you've come so far and have so much to lose that the drama of the game world is always gripping. How many times in other games have you been warned by some Cortana knockoff "Oh no, a wave of dangerous and battle-hardened foes is approaching, try not to poop your pants!" only to be faced by more of the same goons you've been absent-mindedly mowing down for hours? This never happens in Kenshi. Kenshi never has to artificially inflate the stakes, because the stakes are always real. Kenshi never has to script its drama, because its drama is generated automatically by your interactions with the world.

Once you've got past the rocky start, the dodgy presentation, the occasional wonkiness of the AI, and the overall hostility of the world, the freedom the developers promise really is there. You choose your own adventures and your own goals; there are fights to be had, rivals to be made, bounties to be collected, factions to befriend or destroy, and a surprisingly deep city-building element you can pick up or ignore completely as you see fit. Kenshi will reward all the time, imagination, and obsession you pour into it - just give it a chance!

I bought this game 6 days ago and I have already lost 33 hours to it, and I feel like I haven't scratched the surface yet. I started off with the goal of being a humble smith, levelled some stats, got some groupies, adopted a bonedog pup named Wonko, things were good.

The game is absolutely amazing in every way, the only thing that holds it back imo is the UI.
That having been said, here are some important shortcuts to deal with it more effectively when starting out:

Spacebar - Pause
F2 / F3 / F4 - Slow down / Speed up game time
1 - 9 - Quick character selection 
Left Alt - Highlights items on the floor
C - Stats of currently selected character
I - Inventory of currently selected character
M - Map
B - Build mode

Also, one last note:
Avoid save scumming!
Kenshi heavily revolves around the player making up their own story, so for a better experience, try resisting the urge to load previous saves when something unexpected happens.

Have fun!

I figured that after almost 200 hours of playing I should post a review. Kenshi is a unique game. It has base building elements of Stronghold and Age of Empires set in a post apocalyptic world similar to fallout but in Japan with ninjas. Your characters are similar to Sims where you can directly control everything they do like eat, sleep, work, craft, train, fight, loot, build, explore, and trade just to name a few. You can equip gear(weapons, clothing, armor, backpacks, accessories, and robotic limbs) to each of your characters. You typically start with one character and sometimes a pet, but you will want to recruit as many characters/pets as you are able to feed. I like the jobs aspect where you can assign them a list of different jobs to perform in order of most important to the least. It really comes in handy when you have 50+ characters and you are running essentially an entire city. When you start just know that everything can and probably will kill you. You typically start as a weakling with no skills, barely any clothes, usually no friends, and probably just a stick to defend yourself. 

As I mentioned you start with one character, however your objective is basically to survive. Your characters will level up by performing tasks for example if you run, your athletics skill will increase etc. What is so different about this game is how the characters react to damage. If you take damage to your characters left arm, your character will hold that arm like it hurts. They will also not be able to perform certain tasks 100% until that arm is bandaged up and healed. Your characters can also lose limbs completely and be forced to crawl to safety (if they don't bleed to death) or become enslaved etc. 

There are different races and factions within the game, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. There are also legendary bosses in game, think Age of Empires meets Shadow of the Colossus. Doing things (selling things, collecting bounties, buying things, etc) for each faction will increase your standing with them and they are less likely to enslave or kill you. 

Crafting is pretty simple where you find or buy books or blueprints that you use for research points to unlock new things to build/craft for your base. There are prospecting elements as well, some areas are more fertile than others for different crops. Like cactus grows better in the desert etc. Water is not available everywhere, you have to find it and task a character to draw it out of a well that you build to water your crops.

I played the base game for about 40 or 50 hours before I discovered the mods in the workshop... Graphics, animations, quests, armors, weapons, character customization, base building, etc are all way better with mods. Please don't judge this game from the video on steam. Buy it, play it for a little bit to get the hang of it, then find the mods that you want to make the game customized for you. This is basically the ultimate sandbox game where you can do whatever you want. I usually start a base. I will raise an army to attack which ever faction attacked me first. Just remember that shifting the balance of the factions have consequences... Loads of fun if you have the patience to start from nothing. 

There are a lot of ways to survive in Kenshi and each time you play will be completely unique. There are so many layers to Kenshi that I could probably write a book. Totally worth $29.99 if you like sandbox games.

So I've played this game over 1,000 hours, and I mean it is fun and which is why I'm giving it a positive review. But that's about the only reason.

In reality, this game is still riddled with bugs. So much so the devs added a feature that basically lets you reset the whole game world once it inevitably becomes messed up. Of course while you do have some control over what resets, there're a lot of things you want to carry over when you do that simply won't.
 
As for actual patches, the devs seem more focused on patching potential exploits and making cosmetic changes before addressing actual bugs that have been in the game for over a year. To this day, if you want to start a new game while you're playing, you have to completely close the application, relaunch it, and select 'new game' from the title screen. Because if you try to use the 'new game' button in the in-game menu, it'll mess up trying to load a new map, which can result in towns spawning with nobody in them. Oh and you still can't go back to the title screen either. Meanwhile they updated the position of the buildings in the starting town 3 times, for no reason. And every update seems to change what recruits you can find where.

What makes things more frustrating is when you try to report bugs (that are obviously bugs) and get responses from players telling you how it doesn't bother them, or to just ignore it, or they try to use flimsy logic to explain that its clearly a feature (like having your base randomly disappear if you're away from it too long). And if you're real lucky, someone'll tell you that there's a mod to fix it so there's no need for the devs to waste their time doing it themselves, so stop acting so entitled.

Other than that, for a fully released game, there're still a lot features in this game that just feel unfinished. The overall map feels like the devs spent most of their time on the Eastern half of the map, and as they moved West they just kind of got bored and called it a day.

I don't mean to be harsh, the game really is fun, and I do recommend it. But the devs need to work more on making it functional and less on cosmetic changes.

Kenshi is glitchy. The base-building system is the jankiest thing I've ever encountered, and I've come across so many irritating bugs that they've made me want to smash my laptop against a wall.

And I cannot. Get. Enough.

Kenshi is brutal and doesn't care if you're terrible at it. Everyone is trying to kill you, and you start as an absolute nobody with no skills (depending on your starting choice). There are no quests or objectives—you're essentially creating your own story, and it works unbelievably well.

What makes Kenshi so incredibly rewarding is how it encourages you to persevere. Got beaten up and robbed? Time to get up and get beaten up again. Each time you lose a fight, you grow a little stronger, until you can topple entire nations single-handedly and become an absolute god. You can replace your limbs with high-tech robotics that let you run at 50+ mph with superhuman strength—if you want. I seem to build an army of cyborg god-beings every playthrough.

You don't have to be a fighter (though it helps). You can be a farmer, trader, robotics expert, assassin, smith, thief, or all of the above. Want characters who specialize in specific skills? The game is squad-based, so you can control multiple characters, build a base, create a self-sustaining town, or go completely solo. The world is your oyster.

Kenshi has an active modding community, so if anything about the game isn't to your taste, there's likely a mod to fix it.

This is one of my all-time favorite games, and I wish I could experience it for the first time again. I'm recommending it to anyone who hasn't played it—experience this broken masterpiece for yourself.

The best way I can describe this game (or at least how I felt about it) is that it's similar to having a bunch of action figures and making stories by playing with them. You all know what I mean, when you were a kid you would play with dolls or action figures and make little stories around it and you could get lost for hours with that. That's Kenshi for me. I started a few playthroughs but failed multiple times because I didn't know what I was doing until I actually read up a bit online and played for a good 50ish hours, then I started my main playthrough where I "finished" the game. The Monks of the Fist

His name was Oji, he was part of an isolated village that practiced the ancient art of meditation and martial arts. However, one day the village was discovered and raided by the United Cities mistaking them for a far off Holy Nation farm. Oji was the only one who escaped and found refuge in the borderzone, well away from nobles eye's. He was devastated and felt survivors guilt. He would roam the Shek kingdoms with the voices of his village shouting at him. He worked for hours by mining iron to distract from the noise, walking with tons of iron on his back, it didn't help. One day he attacked a Shek guard and was beaten to a pulp and thrown in jail, he survived and stayed in that jail for weeks. He contemplated what had happened and remembered what his master taught. TLDR: Souls like games are good because they're built with the assumption that the player will lose a lot, especially early on, and are balanced in a way that makes repeated attempts rewarding and not overly penalizing. Kenshi is great because it's built with the assumption that you will lose a lot, but rather than minimizing consequences it makes those consequences the sort of thing that you can work through and grow from, even making those loses rewarding enough that experienced players aren't even attempted to load a previous save. Rather than forcing the player to constantly save and reload, kenshi stews the player in each loss while allowing every defeat to be an experience worth having. 


Full review:
A short tale about the glorious pain of playing kenshi:

Your character was ambushed by bandits, you've lost all your equipment and now you're starving to death. Both legs are crippled so you can't walk, crawling to the nearest city is the only chance you have left to squeeze out a tight save before you bleed out. 

But then slavers find you, beat you a few inches closer to death, and carry you to a work camp in shackles. you made a save file, so time to restart right?

Wrong

The slavers shave your head and bandage your wounds. With a little time, you heal up and even unarmed you can find your way out of the slave camp. Will you fail? Probably. Shackles slowed you down the first time, the guards beat you down before you reached the gate. But they heal you again, put you back to work, and next time you pick the lock on the shackles first and tear them off before fleeing. 

A few more cycles of this and finally you break out. Maybe you free the other prisoners first, loot weapons and fight your way out together. Maybe you sneak out in the middle of the night, knocking out a couple guards on your way. Or maybe you just picked a good time and booked it out of there. Now you're running into the sunset, making your way for more distant lands where you aren't marked as a fugitive, at least until you can grow your hair back out and lose the attention of local slavers.

And all those beatings, the running around and the hard labor, it made you stronger. You're starving, but after you get some food in you your character is a bigger, better, faster version of the one that was carried off into a slave camp. Hell, maybe you lost an arm, but you can replace with with a new, shiny prosthetic that can punch a bandit's skull in with one hit. One day you'll come back even stronger, with a squad of real heavy hitters, and you'll burn that camp to the ground before moving on to tearing down the entire country. 

Welcome to kenshi.

In any other game you would have save scummed, because if losing has any consequences at all they're something you want to avoid. But kenshi doesn't play like that: losing hurts, and it has consequences that completely change the path of the game, but there's almost always a way forward so loading a save usually isn't necessary, in fact you'll probably come out better if you let the scenario play out. 

Dark souls is hard: there's a high skill ceiling that kicks your ass at first but builds you up in a way that will have you starting a new file and dancing around enemies until you're beating the final boss with no armor and a starting weapon without taking a hit, because it's a game you're meant to be able to master. 

Kenshi is PAINFUL: you will never escape that pain, it's in the fabric of the game itself, a feature that builds the core experience. You can manage it, get much better at dealing with it, but the pain will always be there even after you "master" it.

Like a souls game, losing is not a deal breaker that forces you to load up a save, but rather than removing the consequences kenshi renegotiates the consequences to be ones you can move on and grow from.

This game is difficult to get into. It drops you into a vast world basically naked and afraid. You start at level 1, the bottom of the barrel. You are not a hero, and you are not special. You're just another person in a vast canvas that is Kenshi. 

The tutorials give you the very bare necessities to get going, basic information to survive. But nothing more. There isn't an objective, no quest. You just exist to make of it what you want. It's like a living sandbox. It's daunting at first, I had no idea what to do. I chose the wanderer (default experience, the dev says "is the way it's meant to be played". I wandered outside of the city and was immediately murdered by wildlife. Alright, start a new game. Enter a building to start training on a dummy to level up my skills, apparently I wasn't allowed to be there. Get whooped by guards and imprisoned. Live out my sentence, back at it. Try to kill some wildlife to get furs, trade for some meager coins, get some basic resources and make a camp. Cook food, alright, at least now Im not starving. 

Slowly as I prodded and poked the game, learning by trial and error, I eventually recruited some homies and started an outpost. Now I have a mining op, I trade regularly with the local city for resources, and am slowly living out a story that presented itself as naturally as could be.

I can feel the depth of this game just below the surface. There's so much left to learn and explore. The mechanics aren't terribly complex once you start to understand the core principals of the game. There's just a lot of it, and the game is exceptionally unique. It's difficult if not impossible to apply experience from other games to this one (with some exceptions) as it's irrelevant.

Key takeaways if you choose to play this game (which I definitely recommend):
- You are not significant, you will die, or be captured, maimed and left for dead. It's part of the experience.
- This isn't Dark Souls, it's not meant to be hard just to be hard. It's hard because life in Kenshi is hard. This world is barren, it's cold (metaphorically, so far it's been nothing but desert), and uncaring. Be cautious as you explore.
- It's a pure RPG, skills are gained by performing relevant actions. A solid strategy to get your toughness perk up (basic defense stats) is to get into fights you can't win, but wont kill you. Basically go punch a big guy, get whooped, heal, repeat until you've toughened up.
- There are no restrictions, do whatever you want. Nothing is gated behind quests. You wanna go try and raid a city? Do it. Want to align with a faction? Go collect bounties. Whatever you wanna do, just remember, you aren't special. You have no advantage over NPCs just by being the main character from your perspective.
- Mods, there's lots of them. I don't believe in the "play it vanilla first, it's the best way" gatekeep-y stupidity. Check them out, use them as you want. I chose some obvious QoL mods. W/e, the game is meant to be whatever you make of it.
- Armor and weapon stats are a little confusing, be cautious about gearing up with lots of armor, it may not be as helpful as you think.
- Friends are always good, solo play is definitely a thing, but your chances of survival dramatically increase with friends (NPCs, this game is strictly singleplayer).

This is the sandboxiest sandbox game I've played. It really is a game that says "here's a world, here's your character. Go forth and do whatever you want." It's not a game intended for people who want a game to tell you what to do with clear objectives. There are none. Just to exist and stake your claim in the world.

I remember when I first got this game, back in summer of '13. I had started out with nothing but the clothes on my back, some cash, and a rusty sword. 

First thing to do was to find some buddies to help, and so I went to the nearest town. In a tavern I met a short bald man (though we were all bald back then). His name was Dirt, and this was my new best friend. Dirt and I did some pretty bad things then, luring guards to get killed by starving bandits, and then stealing all of the gear. This changed when we both got a little close one fight, and got chased by bandits all the way into the entrance of town. There weren't enough men to hold them all back, so I went into a tavern to see if anyone could help. I found a huge man, named Vedi. Vedi was willing to help for a price, and after paying him he went out there with a rusty sword and killed 3 of the bandits before he passed out from blood loss, effectively saving the town.

It was the three of us for a good, long time. We killed many a cannibal and a bandit, and soon enough came upon the idea to make our own outpost, a safe haven to keep us secure and resupply when the going got tough. There was a town nearby, so all we had to do was get a few materials here and there and after a week maybe it would be set. By this time all three of us were pretty decked out, myself having a good long coat, Vedi with a huge cleaver, and Dirt with a tricorn hat. Most cannibals were either afraid of us by this point, or dead, there wasn't much worry of our safety by now. 

We had almost finished the small base, with Vedi and I working on some some construction, so it was Dirt's turn to go get the materials. We had both finished our construction, and so had waited for Dirt to come back. A day had gone by, we were starting to get worried. By noon the next day, Vedi and I had decided to risk it and leave the base, to go see where Dirt had gone. The next town over must surely know where he went?

We didn't even make it halfway across when we found him, laying on the ground. 

His hat and sword weren't far from him, and there were two dead bandits next to him. Incisions and cuts were all across his body, bones broken and blood everywhere. Vedi cried, I stared for a good long time, before getting his hat and sword. I walked to the nearest bandit encampment, which some members looked wounded, and slaughtered them all with Vedi, after he finally caught up.

Time has passed since that day, and the small base we had thought of originally is now a bustling town, with nearly eight residents there, all dressed and ready to defend their home. These people are the best I could have asked for, and I still keep the tricorn hat as a symbol of office, with Vedi forgoeing his cleaver for that sword, as his symbol of guard captain. But as much as I love these people, and would die for them, they will never be that man whom Vedi and I came to know as our best friend.

R.I.P. Dirt.

This game is very close to the "perfect game" I envisioned in my head after reading very early hype material for the "Tabula Rasa" mmo way back when.

Ever since then, faction warfare and the chance of factions taking over areas they are fighting over has been a gaming kink for me.
Kenshi has this and more. It also has its flaws (a lot of them), but the core concept is there and it makes the less functional bits easier to gloss over.

Much like Rimworld or Dwarf Fortress, this game is built on losses. Or rather, the story for your playthrough is built on losses. You are not expected to play perfectly. Instead, you are expected to get by, by the skin of your teeth.

In my first game I spent my starting money on food (I started as a Wanderer) and was forced to exit the safe haven of my starting settlement to look for ways to survive and get food or money, I got jumped by a band of starving bandits the very first day on the outside of the walls. They beat me to a pulp and stole my food.
I reloaded, and avoided them. This was my reaction after playing a whole lot of other games, where any small defeat is considered "wrong" and you load your previous save. This is also NOT the way I would approach Kenshi any more. I am not going to tell YOU how to play the game, but I would at least recommend going in mostly blind (perhaps look up some of the crafting stuff once you get to that point, since they're not explained intuitively in the ingame tutorials) and try to save-scum as little as possible.


You get beat up, but if it doesn't kill you, it will only make you stronger (well, tougher, but yeah).
The thing is, you want to get beat up, but just safely and without getting eaten or killed afterwards. You want to get some combat experience. Your character grows and learns every time they are doing any kind of action in the game. If they get beat up, then the next time they will be able to take more punishment (as long as they survive this fight).

Sometimes a character dies. That is ok. It is a major loss, especially if this was an important character to your party - BUT - this also makes the game so much more fun to play.

I don't think I've had this much fun playing an emergent RPG in years.
I've had an entire scouting party knocked out and robbed. I've had my pack animals butchered and eaten by bandits. I've had my upstart settlement sacked by 3 bandit factions at the same time, and then on top of it all they arrested my faction leader (my start character) and strapped her up on my own prisoner pole...
This last one was a real pickle to solve, but it's incredible what you can do with some lone survivors, a few thousand Cats and some mercenary groups. The stories you get from a loss is much more enjoyable than the stories you get from "smooth-sailing".

TLDR:
Anyway, point being, I absolutely love this game, despite its flaws (which I intentionally haven't mentioned here. If I mention the flaws now, you will look for them when playing and get a confirmation bias. If I don't mention them, you might not even think about it).
The emergent gameplay here is something very few games get right, and Kenshi is very close to getting it right.

An excellent game to lose yourself in, a heavy focus on how you're just another person in this world but seemingly people miss that anyone can be powerful too as a result of this. So wandering about, you might just find your doom laying in a corner looking like an unassuming person who suddenly wrecks you entirely or if you survive long enough, you are the unassuming doom of predatory people.

In terms of gameplay, everything is determined by statistics and skill levels with your characters acting similarly to an NPC you can direct. Armour and melee weapons are the main focus of gameplay with ranged weapons being a rare annoyance unless you are assaulting a base with turret defences or using any yourself.

Kenshi is difficult by default, the way you get stronger in this game is having the tar kicked out of you and surviving. The stronger the enemy you face and the more poorly equipped you are, the harder this is to do and if you are downed to slavers... enjoy your new life mining ores until you can break out. It is entirely possible to be a wandering ronin or a group of rock hard mercs kicking the hell of out of evil wherever you find it. You can base build, ignore base building and buy buildings in established cities by other factions and not have to worry about defence beyond if the city itself is completely overrun.

Food and medicine are your primary concerns along with becoming ever stronger to fight a very hostile world. If that sounds like a game you'd enjoy, give it a go. It does have jank to it, a clunky glitchiness but I find this adds to the appeal of the game rather than detracts.

Kenshi is one of my favorite games ever made. When I first played it, I went in knowing nothing and was puzzled at the lack of direction (even with the small tutorial you get at the start). 
Like many others, I walked into the hub and tried talking to people, interacting with everything and not getting anywhere. Where were the quests? What was my next objective? The game simply seemed aimless.
I eventually wandered out and found some copper nodes. By selling this copper I was able to buy some food. My stats improved as I hauled copper to the hub and ran back. I got slightly better weapons and slightly better armor.
Then I ran into a couple dust bandits. They tried to extort me, but I wasn't going to let this villainy stand. I initiated combat. It didn't take long to realize I was going to lose the fight, but it was too late to run. I ended up bleeding out on the ground and died. After that frustration, I put down the game.
Fast forward a couple years. I got a better computer and decided to try Kenshi again. This time I was a bit more careful and made the good decision to hire some more folks for my crew. Eventually I came up with a system of improving my fighting skills but staying alive by leaving a medic out of the battles to heal everyone at the end. I was already starting to enjoy the progression of gearing and leveling my party while accruing wealth, but the game hadn't fully "clicked" for me yet.
That all changed when I came upon a town, accidentally ignited a gang war, and stole the merchandise from dead shopkeepers. I gained a small fortune and made a base. My stats increased, I was crafting my own items, farming, raiding labs and improving my technology. I was thriving.
I traveled the vast world, met all the major factions, making friends and enemies along the way. Squad members were gained and lost. Glorious loot and top tier weapons and armor were treasure. I joined a cause and became a freedom fighter.

I barely touched upon the intricacies, charm, and aesthetics of this indie game in my review, but I hope you get the picture. The game opened my eyes to a new way of play that is more personal and self-driven than a simple linear story driven (or even open world quest driven) game. The freedom gave its own satisfaction.
Don't get me wrong, the developers of this game (seriously brilliant) knew what they were doing. They accounted for tons of scenarios and ways of playing, but it never feels forced. The game is not easy because even when you reach a point of success in something, the next lofty goal you work towards will be exponentially harder (yet achievable). It keeps you engaged knowing you are working to fulfil your dream.

I look forward to the release of Kenshi 2, but even after all these years there are things in this game I have yet to do, but I am thoroughly enjoying the journeys along the way.

Great game.

Pros
- complex world
- lots to explorer
- interesting locations
- light story (the world is set in it's way, but you can change some major things if you know how)
- interesting characters (Beep for example, love him)
- combat is cruel and unforgiving
- starting off is brutal (experience at the game radically changes this however)
- knowledge of locations/game mechanics is the difference between success and failure (experience)
- no black and white factions, every faction has complexity of good and evil (even the Holy Nation can save your life and be kind/warm, assuming you are a Human male)
- Shidan. This is a person not in the game nor a dev. He's a forum mod who has a deep understanding of the game and it's mechanics, he makes game mods for Kenshi that really improve the game experience as do his efforts on the forums. Great guy. 

Cons
- world lacks depth where it'd be expected
- questions about the world lack answers from lore available (can be good too I guess, lots of threads discussing lore)
- Hive Soldiers still suck because of the helmet slot (I made so many posts about this, the meta supports this)
- Samurai Armor is overpowered, the armor rebalance that took place made it vastly superior to all other heavy armor as well as most medium armor (meta supports this)

On the fence issues
- certain weapons are just plain bad (which is realistic I guess)
- martial arts is insanely overpowered with 90+ stats with blows landing for possibly 200-450+ damage (it takes forever to build to that point so I guess it's okay) only 1 npc has this (explained by lore) it's a players choice otherwise
- base building is a optional feature that ranges from impossible to making the player OP with unlimited resources. the middle range is very fun.

Final thoughts and warnings

The game is a total pain in the ass to learn but I found it rewarding. It doesn't hold your hand (or even do a good job explaining the mechanics) and you will be put in unwinnable situations by bad luck.

Advice for new players
- run away from stuff if it looks like you can't win, don't wait till your legs are crippled
- everyone is stronger then you when start, join in on fights where 1 party is winning and is neutral (not neutral bandits as they might decide to attack you). the first few skill ups are hard to get and dangerous to get, even 1 starving bandit is stronger then you by a lot
- don't steal gear for downed members of major factions, if they see you do it you will regret it
- run away when uncertain
- run away

Getting downed once can cause you to bleed out, game over. Getting hurt is good to build stats, bandage heal, rinse and repeat. Getting hurt and escaping is a win. Once you get the stats things start to change and you control the combat.

"You know when a game looks like sh*t, it's gonna be good" once said a wise man. That's Kenshi for you. A British guy says "I'm gonna make the ultimate game." And he works on it for 12 years, 6 years of it being alone. And he does it. Chris' story is exactly how this game works.

You're not special, you're not a chosen one, but you can make yourself one through hard work. There's no story or quests yet there's so much more to do than those games that do have them. It's a game made for hardcore and patient gamers. 

Thought you could attack some goats for food and get away with it?  Nope, goats will break your legs if you don't know how to hold a sword. Thought you could wipe out a bandit camp all on your own at the very beginning? You'll be lucky if you can kill a single one of them. Thought a dragon would save you from being a prisoner? You'll die from work if you don't do something to get yourself out. Thought you could build a base out in the wilderness and be left alone? Nope, you'll have to pay tax to soil's owner. Thought paying tax would get you protection? It won't! You'll be attacked by people that are so hungry that they lost their minds, cannibals, wild creatures, bandits, ancient robots, et cetera, et cetera. And they'll chew through your base. They'll chew through everything you worked so hard for. They'll knock your friends out. They'll knock you out. And you'll consider yourself lucky if they capture you and put you in a cage instead of leaving you to bleed to your death, or heck, eat you alive. And these are a mere 1% of the whole experience you'll go through.

Long story short, if you're a person that values graphics and awesome gameplay, stay away from this game. But if you're a person that loves an incredibly immersive, challenging game that doesn't hold your hand, get this masterpiece.
